title.en: Soma and Rudra, the makers of weal, and the lord of the fords

summary: Seventeen yajus, each a namaḥ with one or two names in the dative. Sāyaṇa introduces them as further yajus with namaḥ on one side, continuing anuvāka 7. They name Rudra as Soma and Rudra, the red sun, the bringer of weal and lord of creatures, the fierce slayer near and far, the green-haired trees and the deliverer; then as the source and maker of happiness (śambhu, mayobhu, śaṅkara, mayaskara), the auspicious and more auspicious; and last as present at fords and banks, at the far and near shore, at the crossing over and out, and in the river's grass, foam, sand and stream, which Sāyaṇa reads as the crossing of saṃsāra and as Rudra in the form of the faithful who live by the rivers.

vyakarana.note: Dative with namaḥ (‘homage to …’), as is every name in this anuvāka. Sāyaṇa does not take soma here as the soma plant or its god: he analyses it as sa + umā, ‘he who is together with Umā’ (a vigraha of the saha-bahuvrīhi kind). The word itself is the ordinary soma, and the text gives no compound to divide.
The pattern of the anuvāka is namaḥ X ca Y ca: one namaḥ and two names, each followed by ca, ‘both to X and to Y’. Sāyaṇa counts each such line as one yajus.

translation.literal: Homage both to Soma and to Rudra.
translation.readable: Homage to Soma and to Rudra.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa introduces the anuvāka as further yajus with namaḥ on one side only, continuing those of anuvāka 7 (कानिचिदन्यतरतोनमस्काराण्यष्टमेऽनुवाके कथ्यन्ते), and counts seventeen of them (सप्तदश यजूंष्याह). He explains soma as ‘he who is together with Umā’, and rudra by derivation: rud is weeping, its cause is sorrow, and Rudra is the one who drives that sorrow away.

flags.note: soma is the name Soma in the dictionaries (Keith: ‘Homage to Soma’); Sāyaṇa reads it as sa + umā, ‘with Umā’. The translation keeps the name; the word table gives his reading.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes both colours as Rudra in the form of the sun (āditya): tāmra, deep red at the moment of rising, and aruṇa, still reddish after it has risen.

vyakarana.note: agre ‘in front’ and dūre ‘far off’ are locatives that keep their case ending inside the compound (aluk); vadha is ‘striking, slaying’. Monier-Williams: agrevadha ‘hitting or killing whatever is in front’, dūrevadha ‘far-striking’.

translation.readable: Homage to him who strikes what stands before him, and to him who strikes from afar.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa analyses agrevadha as ‘he whose striking is in front, before him’, and dūrevadha likewise; the sense, he says, is that Rudra slays an opponent without effort, whether the opponent stands before him or far away.

vyakarana.note: Agent noun in -tṛ from the root han ‘to strike, slay’; dat. sg. hantre.
Comparative in -īyas formed directly from the root han (as garīyas, jyāyas): ‘slaying more, the greater slayer’; dat. sg. hanīyase.

translation.literal: Homage both to the slayer and to the greater slayer.
translation.readable: Homage to the slayer, and to the one who slays still more.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: in the world too, whoever slays an opponent anywhere, it is Rudra in that form who is the slayer (hantṛ). For this he cites the Lord's words to Arjuna: by me they have already been slain; be only the occasion, Savyasācin. He is hanīyas, the greater slayer, because at the time of dissolution he slays all, in the highest degree.

vyakarana.note: Plural: the homage goes to the trees themselves. This yajus has no ca: one namaḥ, a noun and the adjective that agrees with it.
hari ‘green, yellowish, tawny’ + keśa ‘hair’; a bahuvrīhi in apposition to vṛkṣebhyaḥ. Monier-Williams: harikeśa ‘fair-headed’.

translation.literal: Homage to the trees, the green-haired [ones].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes the hair as the leaves: the trees whose leaves, green in colour, are like hair — the wish-granting kalpa tree and the others — and the sense is that Rudra is in their form.

vyakarana.note: tāra, from tṝ ‘to cross’: ‘carrying across, a saviour’ (Monier-Williams, citing the parallel of this mantra in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi.40). The yajus is the single word with namaḥ; Sāyaṇa counts it as one of the seventeen.

translation.literal: Homage to the one who carries across.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: tāra is the one made known by the praṇava, the syllable om.

flags.note: The dictionaries give tāra ‘carrying across, saviour’ here (Keith: ‘the deliverer’); Sāyaṇa explains it as the one denoted by the praṇava. Monier-Williams also records tāra as a name of the syllable om in later texts. The translation gives the sense of the word; the traditional note gives Sāyaṇa's.

vyakarana.note: śam (indecl.) ‘weal, happiness’ + -bhu from bhū ‘to be, come to be’; dat. sg. of the u-stem, with guṇa: śambhave.

mayas ‘refreshment, delight’ + -bhu; inside the compound -as becomes -o before the voiced bh. Monier-Williams gives the stem as mayobhu or mayobhū; the dative mayobhave is that of the short u-stem, like śambhave.

translation.literal: Homage both to the source of weal and to the source of delight.
translation.readable: Homage to him from whom weal comes, and to him from whom delight comes.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: śambhu brings śam, happiness, into being; mayobhū brings mayas, happiness, into being. He distinguishes the two: the one is the happiness of the objects of sense, the other the happiness of liberation.

vyakarana.note: mayas + kara ‘making’ (from kṛ). Inside the compound the final s of mayas stands before k (mayaskara), not visarga. Monier-Williams: ‘causing enjoyment, giving pleasure’.

translation.literal: Homage both to the maker of weal and to the maker of delight.
translation.readable: Homage to him who makes weal, and to him who makes delight.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: śaṅkara makes worldly happiness, in the form of a father and the like; mayaskara makes the happiness of liberation, in the form of the teacher, the scriptures and the like. These two words, he says, state that Rudra makes happiness directly; the previous two (śambhu, mayobhū), that he has it made through these.

vyakarana.note: pāra ‘the far bank’ + -ya; avārya from avāra ‘the near bank’. Monier-Williams: pārya ‘being on the opposite side or bank’, avārya ‘being on the near side of a river’.

translation.literal: Homage both to the [one] on the far bank and to the [one] on the near bank.
translation.readable: Homage to him on the farther shore, and to him on the nearer.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes pāra as the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, where Rudra abides as the one on whom those who seek liberation meditate. In the bhāṣya as transmitted this sentence runs straight on into the word avārya, so his separate gloss on the near bank cannot be read there. On anuvāka 11 Sāyaṇa quotes the Brāhmaṇa's rule that the Rudra offering is made in three parts, and says that the second part ends with avāryāya ca.

flags.note: corrections.json (N8.13): the second witness reads अवार्त्याय; the text keeps अवार्याय, the counterpart of pārya (W2 error).

Sāyaṇa's gloss on pārya and avārya appears to have lost words in transmission: the sentence explaining the far shore ends with ‘… is avārya’. The word table follows the plain sense of avāra, the near bank.

a + u → o (ād guṇaḥ, P. 6.1.87)

vyakarana.note: pra + taraṇa (from tṝ ‘to cross’, with the suffix -ana): ‘carrying forward, crossing over’; ut-taraṇa, ‘crossing out of, coming out across’. Both are used as names in the dative.

translation.literal: Homage both to the [one who] carries over and to the [one who] brings out across.
translation.readable: Homage to him who carries across, and to him who brings out to the other side.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: prataraṇa is the cause of crossing over sin, in the form of the repetition of mantras and the like; uttaraṇa is the cause of crossing out of the whole of saṃsāra, in the form of the knowledge of reality. On anuvāka 11 he says that the third of the three parts of the Rudra offering begins with this yajus.

words.meaning: to the one connected with the alāda
words.context: Sāyaṇa: alāda is the jīva, which eats the fruit of action to the full; Rudra is alādya as its impeller
ca … ca, ‘both … and’: each ca follows the word it adds

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y (P. 8.3.17), which is dropped (P. 8.3.19), leaving the hiatus
a + a → ā (akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ, P. 6.1.101)

vyakarana.note: ā-tāra (from tṝ with ā, ‘a crossing to, landing’) + -ya. Monier-Williams: ātārya ‘relating to landing’.

Sāyaṇa derives the stem from alāda, ‘one who eats (ad) fully (alam)’, + -ya ‘connected with’. ca + a- and ca + ā- both give cā-, so the junction alone does not decide between alādya and ālādya; Sāyaṇa's alāda decides it. Monier-Williams has no entry for the word.

translation.literal: Homage both to the [one] of the crossing back and to the [one] connected with the eater [of the fruit of action].
translation.readable: Homage to him of the return crossing, and to him who is bound up with the one who tastes the fruit of action.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: even when the knowledge of reality that carries one out of saṃsāra is at hand, a man may set it aside and, by performing rites for desired ends, come back again into saṃsāra; that return is ātāra, and the one who merits it is ātārya — that is, the giver of the fruits of desire-prompted rites. alāda is the jīva, which eats the fruit of action to the full, as the śruti he quotes says: ‘one of the two eats the sweet fig’. Rudra, being its impeller and so connected with it, is alādya.

flags.note: corrections.json (N8.15): the second witness reads आलाट्याय; the text keeps -lādya (W2 error). The note there cites Sāyaṇa's alāda, ‘one who eats the fruit of action’.

The padaccheda is अलाद्याय, after Sāyaṇa's derivation from alāda; the Saṃhitā चालाद्याय would equally be ca + ālādya. Sāyaṇa's own sentence, as transmitted, ends तत्संबन्धित्वा दालद्यः, which is not clean: it could stand for -tvād alādyaḥ or for a derivative ālādya. The padaccheda rests on his alāda and on the collation note in corrections.json, which reads alādya.
ātārya is ‘relating to landing’ in Monier-Williams (Keith: ‘him of the crossing’); Sāyaṇa reads ātāra as the return into saṃsāra through rites done for desired ends.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: śaṣpa is young grass, the shoots of kuśa and the like that grow on the banks of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, and śaṣpya is the one worthy of it (tad arhati, he says, for all four names); phenya, the one worthy of the foam in the middle of the river.

vyakarana.note: sikatā ‘sand’ + -ya (the final ā dropped before the suffix); pravāhya from pravāha ‘current, stream’. The anuvāka ends here (॥) at the pañcāśat mark [18].

translation.literal: Homage both to the [one] in the sand and to the [one] in the current.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: sikatya is the one worthy of the sand, pravāhya the one worthy of the current. The purport of the four names śaṣpya, phenya, sikatya and pravāhya, he says, is Rudra in the form of the person of faith, intent on bathing and the like, who lives always on the banks of the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
